{{for|the theorem about midpoints of a quadrangle|Varignon's theorem}}

'''Varignon's theorem''' is a theorem of French mathematician [[Pierre Varignon]] (1654–1722), published in 1687 in his book ''Projet d'une nouvelle mécanique''. The theorem states that the [[torque]] of a [[Euclidean vector#Addition and subtraction|resultant]] of two [[resultant force|concurrent forces]] about any point is equal to the [[algebraic sum]] of the torques of its components about the same point. 
In other words, "If many [[Concurrent lines|concurrent]] forces are acting on a body, then the algebraic sum of torques of all the forces about a point in the plane of the forces is equal to the torque of their resultant about the same point."<ref name="gbooks">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=pe_QRJ6wOtEC&q=Varignon+theorem+mechanics&pg=PA86 |title=Engineering Mechanics: Statics |author=I. C. Jong, B. G. Rogers |year=1991|publisher=Saunders College Pub. |isbn=9780030263095 }}</ref>

== Proof ==
Consider a set of ''<math>N</math>'' [[force vector]]s <math>\mathbf{f}_1, \mathbf{f}_2, ..., \mathbf{f}_N</math> that concur at a point <math>\mathbf{O}</math> in space. Their resultant is:
[[File:Varignontheoremdiagram.png|alt=|right|400x400px]]
:<math>\mathbf{F}=\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{f}_i </math>.

The torque of each vector with respect to some other point <math>\mathbf{O}_1</math> is

:<math> \mathbf{\Tau}_{O_1}^{\mathbf{f}_i} = (\mathbf{O}-\mathbf{O}_1) \times \mathbf{f}_i </math>.

Adding up the torques and pulling out the common factor <math>(\mathbf{O}-\mathbf{O_{1}})</math>, one sees that the result may be expressed solely in terms of <math> \mathbf{F} </math>, and is in fact the torque of <math> \mathbf{F} </math> with respect to the point <math>\mathbf{O}_1</math>:

:<math> \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{\Tau}_{O_1}^{\mathbf{f}_i}
= (\mathbf{O}-\mathbf{O}_1) \times  \left ( \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbf{f}_{i} \right )
=  (\mathbf{O}-\mathbf{O}_1) \times \mathbf{F}
= \mathbf{\Tau}_{O_1}^{\mathbf{F}} </math>.

Proving  the theorem, i.e. that the sum of torques about <math>\mathbf{O}_1</math> is the same as the torque of the sum of the forces about the same point.
